lessons.title: Core deliverable vs. bonuses
body: An offer is not simply a list of things included in a product. It's a structured collection of deliverables designed to help one specific customer achieve one specific outcome — and customers need to understand that central value before they see everything that comes with it. A stack shown bonuses-first looks like a pile of scattered extras; the same stack shown core-first reads as thoughtful support for one clear promise.

Product, core deliverable, feature, bonus and offer stack
These five words get used loosely, and mixing them up is where most offer stacks go wrong. The product is the complete thing you sell. The core deliverable is the part of it that directly solves the main problem and delivers the outcome from Module 3 — if nothing else existed, this alone would still be the offer. A feature is a component inside the core deliverable itself, not a separate item — it's part of how the core deliverable works, not something you'd list beside it. A bonus is a separate, smaller deliverable that solves a secondary problem the core deliverable doesn't already cover. The offer stack is the whole visible structure: the core deliverable plus its supporting bonuses.

Identifying your core deliverable
A practical method for deciding what belongs in the core:
  1. Revisit your Outcome Statement from Module 3.
  2. Identify the main problem the customer is actually paying to solve.
  3. Identify the essential knowledge, tools, resources or process needed to solve it.
  4. Decide what the customer must receive to reach that outcome — nothing more.
  5. Remove anything that doesn't meaningfully contribute to that one outcome, however useful it seems on its own.
That last step is where most beginners struggle — everything feels relevant to something. The test is whether it contributes to this specific outcome, not whether it's generally good advice:
WEAKER CORE
Content planning templates, a general social media trends report, and a guide to photography lighting.
STRONGER CORE
A step-by-step content-planning process, a content pillar framework, and a weekly planning workflow that turns ideas into finished posts.
The trends report and the lighting guide might both be useful content — but neither one is required to plan a week of posts, so neither belongs in the core.

What makes a good bonus
Bonuses are supplementary deliverables that address relevant secondary problems — not padding to make the box look fuller. A good bonus addresses a real obstacle, supports the main transformation, makes implementation easier, reduces uncertainty or friction, and complements the core deliverable rather than competing with it for attention. A bonus should never exist merely to make the product look bigger: too many unrelated bonuses dilute the offer's central value and make it harder for the customer to see what they're actually buying. DigitalOps still recommends no more than four or five bonuses in total.

Selecting the right bonuses
Go back to your Module 2 Problem Inventory for this — don't invent bonuses from scratch:
  1. Identify the main problem already solved by your core deliverable.
  2. Review the remaining Before, During and After problems in your inventory.
  3. Identify which of those could actually prevent the customer from reaching the intended outcome.
  4. Select the most relevant ones — not every remaining problem needs to become a bonus.
  5. Match each selected problem to one useful supplementary deliverable.
  6. Remove anything redundant or only loosely related.

The core vs. bonus decision test
  • Does the customer need this to receive the main outcome? It likely belongs in the core deliverable.
  • Does it address a related but secondary obstacle? It may be a bonus.
  • Is it just a feature of the core product rather than a separate deliverable? Keep it inside the core — don't list it twice.
  • Does it solve an entirely different major problem? Consider a separate product or offer, not a bonus.
  • Does it require substantial development? Reconsider whether “bonus” is really the right word for it.
A rough “could be built in a few hours” guideline can help as a reference point, but it's not an absolute rule — relevance to the main outcome matters more than production time.

A complete worked example — hypothetical
Continuing with the hypothetical small business owner whose main outcome is “plan and create a week's worth of useful social media content without starting from a blank page every day”:
CORE DELIVERABLE
A practical social media content planning system — a step-by-step planning process, a content pillar framework, a weekly content planning workflow, and instructions for turning ideas into finished posts.
BONUSES → PROBLEM EACH ADDRESSES
Canva social media template pack → difficulty designing posts. Caption-writing worksheet → difficulty writing captions. Weekly content calendar → difficulty organising publishing.
Each bonus earns its place because it solves a specific, named obstacle the core planning system doesn't already remove — design, captions and organising publishing are all real During problems that would otherwise sit unresolved right next to a perfectly good plan. Something that should not be added here: an unrelated personal-finance guide (solves no problem connected to this outcome at all), a complete advanced advertising course (a genuinely different, much larger problem — running ads, not planning content), or a handful of random templates with no clear connection to the core system (padding, not support). These are hypothetical examples, not a real product's actual offer.

Why focused beats oversized
A focused offer with one clear core and a few well-matched bonuses is usually more attractive than an oversized bundle — the customer can see exactly what the price buys and why each piece is there. Every bonus that doesn't clearly connect to the core deliverable dilutes that clarity a little, even if it's individually useful.
lessons.insight: No more than four or five bonuses. Past that point, extra value stops reading as generous and starts reading as padding.

lessons.title: Reduce uncertainty and increase confidence
body:
Even a customer who genuinely wants your outcome can hesitate at the last moment — not because they don't want the result, but because they're uncertain about something specific. Common versions of this uncertainty sound like:
  • “What if this doesn't work for me specifically?”
  • “What if I buy it and don't actually know how to use it?”
  • “What if the material is too advanced — or too basic?”
  • “What if I don't have enough time to follow through?”
  • “What if I pay for something that turns out to be generic?”
A well-designed promise addresses that specific uncertainty without making unrealistic claims. To find which fear actually matters for your offer, don't guess — go back to the evidence:
  1. Return to your Module 2 Problem Inventory.
  2. Review the During and After problems specifically — fear usually lives in “will this actually work for me” territory, not the Before.
  3. Identify which remaining problem creates the greatest uncertainty or perceived risk.
  4. Ask plainly what the customer is afraid will happen if they buy and it doesn't pan out.
  5. Identify what evidence, commitment or reassurance would genuinely address that specific concern.
Your customer's biggest fear should come from this research where possible, not simply be invented at your desk — a hypothetical small business owner's Module 2 research, for instance, might repeatedly surface some version of “I've bought planners before and still didn't know what to actually post,” which points to a very different fear than “I don't have time.”

Full Promise — make a clear, defined commitment
A Full Promise is specific because it commits to something the creator directly controls — not an outcome the creator can't fully guarantee, but a deliverable they absolutely can: “you'll receive 30 editable social media templates, organised into six content categories.” That's credible precisely because delivering 30 templates is entirely within the creator's control, unlike guaranteeing the customer's business will grow. A Full Promise fits best when what you're committing to is the deliverable itself, not a result dependent on circumstances you can't control. A hypothetical fitness coach's version might read “you'll receive a 4-week structured workout calendar with a video demonstration for every exercise” — same logic, different niche: specific, and entirely within the coach's control to deliver.

Conditional Promise — a commitment subject to transparent conditions
A Conditional Promise commits to something only if the customer does their part — which means the conditions must be stated clearly before purchase, not discovered afterward. It needs to say plainly what the customer must do, what the creator commits to if they do it, and the conditions have to be realistic, fair and actually checkable — vague or hidden conditions undermine trust faster than having no guarantee at all. For illustration only: “complete all five weekly planning exercises and submit your final content calendar — if you've followed the process but still can't produce a usable seven-day plan, you can request a review session under the stated programme conditions.” Any real guarantee or remedy you offer must be something you can genuinely deliver, with terms you've actually disclosed — this lesson is not encouraging unrealistic guarantees or misleading refund conditions, only showing the shape a fair one would take.

Confidence Signal — increase trust without guaranteeing an outcome
A Confidence Signal doesn't promise anything — it reduces uncertainty by letting the customer see for themselves. A demonstration is usually more convincing than a claim, because the customer isn't asked to simply trust you. Previews, screenshots, walkthroughs, samples, transparent explanations of exactly how the process works, and genuine testimonials all serve this purpose. A brand-new creator with no testimonials yet isn't stuck here either — showing a preview of the actual product, sharing one sample template, recording a walkthrough of the real workflow, displaying the actual lesson structure, or simply stating plainly what's included and what isn't, all build real trust without needing a single review. What this must never involve is fabricating testimonials, case studies or results — a faked signal, once discovered, destroys more trust than having no proof at all.

Choosing the right type
  • Can you directly control and deliver it? Consider a Full Promise.
  • Are you willing and able to commit to something once clearly stated conditions are met? Consider a Conditional Promise.
  • Is the customer's uncertainty mainly about quality, suitability or how the product actually works? Consider a Confidence Signal.
You don't have to pick only one — an offer can use more than one Promise Type for different purposes at once: a Full Promise about exactly what's included, alongside a Confidence Signal through a real product demonstration. Use whichever combination actually addresses the specific fear you identified above.

Writing your promise statement
  1. Name the customer's biggest fear, specifically — from the method above, not a guess.
  2. Identify what you can genuinely commit to, without overstating it.
  3. Choose the Promise Type (or combination) that fits that commitment.
  4. State the commitment clearly and plainly.
  5. Explain any conditions attached to it.
  6. Remove anything vague, exaggerated or unsupported — read it back and cut what you can't actually back up.
  7. Check that the promise matches the real offer stack — it should describe what you built in Lesson 4.1, not a bigger version of it.
WEAKER
“Guaranteed to transform your business overnight.”
STRONGER
“Get a structured seven-day content planning system, editable templates and guided exercises to help you plan your next week of social media posts.”
The second version is clearer and more credible because every word in it is something the creator can actually deliver — nothing in it needs the customer to simply take their word for it.

A complete worked example — hypothetical
The same hypothetical small business owner identifies their customer's biggest fear as “I'm worried I'll buy another content planner but still won't know what to post.” Addressing it from all three angles:
FULL PROMISE
The product includes a defined content planning system, worksheets and editable templates.
CONDITIONAL PROMISE
Only offered if a genuine, supported implementation commitment actually exists — its terms would need to be explained clearly and fairly. No guarantee is invented here just to fill this section.
CONFIDENCE SIGNAL
A walkthrough showing the planning system turning a blank week into a completed content calendar, start to finish.
Each one addresses a different flavour of the same underlying fear: the Full Promise answers “what exactly am I getting,” the Confidence Signal answers “will this actually work the way it's described,” and a genuine Conditional Promise, where one honestly exists, answers “what happens if it still doesn't click for me.”

Why trust outlasts exaggeration
An exaggerated promise might win a sale today, but it loses the customer's trust the moment reality falls short of it — and that shows up as refund requests, complaints and a damaged reputation, not repeat customers. A promise that's achievable, transparent and genuinely consistent with what you built in Lesson 4.1 earns something more durable than a single purchase: a customer who believes the next thing you say.
lessons.insight: All commitments must be achievable, transparent, and consistent with the actual product or service — a promise that oversells invites refund requests, not sales.

promiseTypes.label: Full Promise
promiseTypes.application: A specific deliverable or service commitment.

promiseTypes.label: Conditional Promise
promiseTypes.purpose: Establish a commitment subject to transparent conditions.
promiseTypes.application: A result or remedy dependent on agreed customer actions.

promiseTypes.label: Confidence Signal
promiseTypes.purpose: Increase trust without guaranteeing an outcome.
promiseTypes.application: Demonstrations, previews, samples, testimonials, support or transparent explanations.

exercise.instructions: List your core deliverable and up to five bonuses, each matched to a problem from your inventory. Then choose a promise type and write your promise statement.

prompts.title: Offer Stack Prompt
prompts.purpose: Use this to find bonuses you'd otherwise miss.
prompts.template: You are a product packaging consultant. My core deliverable: {{m4.coreDeliverable}}. My customer's problem inventory: {{m2.summary}}. For each problem in the "during" and "after" lists that my core deliverable doesn't already solve, suggest one small bonus (not a new big product — something that could realistically be built in under a day) that would resolve it. Suggest no more than 5 bonuses — more than that dilutes the offer. If my core deliverable or problem inventory above is missing or too thin to suggest bonuses confidently, tell me what's missing and ask before suggesting anything. If a bonus idea only works under an assumption about my production capacity or timeline, say so explicitly rather than presenting it as a sure thing. Return a table with three columns: Problem it solves | Bonus name | One sentence describing it.

prompts.title: Promise Builder Prompt
prompts.purpose: Use this to draft a credible promise statement using DigitalOps's three Promise Types.
prompts.template: You are a promise-writing consultant using DigitalOps's three Promise Types — Full Promise (make a clear, defined commitment), Conditional Promise (establish a commitment subject to transparent conditions), and Confidence Signal (increase trust without guaranteeing an outcome). My offer stack: {{m4.summary}}. My target customer's biggest fear or uncertainty about this kind of product: [describe it in your own words before copying this]. Before drafting anything, ask me what I can genuinely commit to delivering, guaranteeing or demonstrating — don't assume capacity I haven't stated. Then suggest one Full Promise option, one Conditional Promise option (only if a genuine condition-based commitment is realistic for me — otherwise say so), and one Confidence Signal option, each addressing the fear above. For each option, draft the actual promise statement and explain in one sentence why it addresses that specific fear. Flag anything in your own drafts that sounds unsupported or exaggerated rather than something I could actually deliver. If my offer stack above is missing or too thin to draft a credible promise, tell me what's missing and ask before drafting anything. Never invent a guarantee, testimonial or result I haven't described to you.
